theme: I cry with my whole heart; your word is my hope
readingInstruction: Read Psalm 119:145-176. This is the last two stanzas of the long acrostic psalm on God’s word. You have read parts of Psalm 119 several times. Today read it as the prayer of a believer in exile, far from home but holding on to the word.
settingTheScene: Psalm 119 is the longest chapter in the Bible, a poem of 176 verses in twenty-two stanzas, one for each letter of the Hebrew alphabet. Every verse speaks of God’s word, using eight or so words for it: law, testimonies, precepts, statutes, commandments, rules, word, and promise. The last stanzas are written as a cry. The psalmist is pursued by persecutors and ends with an image of a lost sheep. It is a good psalm for the exile, as people without a temple clung to the written word.
observation: “With my whole heart I cry; answer me, O LORD! I will keep your statutes” (v. 145).
“I rise before dawn and cry for help; I hope in your words” (v. 147).
“My eyes are awake before the watches of the night, that I may meditate on your promise” (v. 148).
“Those who persecute me with evil purpose draw near; they are far from your law. But you are near, O LORD” (vv. 150-151).
“Long have I known from your testimonies that you have founded them forever” (v. 152).
“The sum of your word is truth, and every one of your righteous rules endures forever” (v. 160).
“Great peace have those who love your law; nothing can make them stumble” (v. 165).
“I have gone astray like a lost sheep; seek your servant, for I do not forget your commandments” (v. 176).
interpretation:
The psalmist prays with his whole heart. He gets up before dawn and stays awake through the night, because his hope is in God’s word. In exile, the word of God was what remained. The temple was gone, the sacrifices ceased, but the written word could still be read, meditated on, and prayed. Many scholars believe the Scriptures became central to Jewish life in exile for this reason.

The situation is not easy. Persecutors are near, but the psalmist notes that “you are near, O LORD.” The enemy is close, but God is closer. The contrast is a source of strength. And he adds, “All your commandments are true.” Even when circumstances are hostile, the word does not change.

There is a beautiful summary in verse 160: “The sum of your word is truth.” The whole is true, and every part is true. The psalmist is not picking out the verses he likes. He has taken all of it. And the result is verse 165: “Great peace have those who love your law.” Peace, shalom, belongs to those who love the word. Nothing makes them stumble.

The last verse is surprising. After 175 verses of praise for the word, the psalmist confesses: “I have gone astray like a lost sheep.” It is an honest ending. He loves the word, and yet he knows he wanders. And his request is, “Seek your servant.” He does not say, “I will find my way back.” He asks the shepherd to find him. The word of God does not make us self-sufficient. It leads us to depend on the God who seeks.
connection: Jesus said, “I am the good shepherd” (John 10:11), and told the story of the shepherd who leaves ninety-nine sheep to seek the one that is lost (Luke 15:3-7). “I have come to seek and to save the lost” (Luke 19:10). 2 Timothy 3:16-17 says that all Scripture is breathed out by God. John 17:17 says, “Your word is truth.” John 14:27 gives Christ’s peace. 1 Peter 2:25: “You were straying like sheep, but have now returned to the Shepherd and Overseer of your souls.”
application:
Set aside time before dawn this week, as the psalmist did, and cry to God from Scripture.

Memorize one verse of Psalm 119 that speaks to your situation.

Pray verse 176 as your own: “Seek your servant.” Thank Jesus for being the shepherd who finds.
prayerPrompts: Cry out to God with your whole heart.
Tell him your hope is in his word.
Thank him that he is near.
